title: Between the testaments
hook: the quieter centuries: Greek rule, then Rome, synagogues everywhere, and people waiting

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Maccabees and the feast of Hanukkah, and your line was rededicate.

Open a King James Bible printed without the Apocrypha, turn to the last page of the Old Testament, and you land in Malachi. Its final verses look forward: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD." Turn one page, and you're in Matthew, with a family tree and a baby. In your hands it's one page. In history it's a long stretch, the gap between the two testaments. Some readers call them the silent years. But they weren't silent. They were waiting years.

First Maccabees opens with Alexander the Great sweeping through and Greek kings ruling the land after him; yesterday's rededicated temple happens in those years. Then Rome arrives. Luke's account of the birth opens with an emperor: "there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed." Meanwhile something quieter grows: the synagogue, a gathering for reading and prayer. In Acts, James says "Moses of old time hath in every city them that preach him, being read in the synagogues every sabbath day." And in Nazareth, Luke says of Jesus, "as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day." A custom, going on long enough to become habit. Through it all, people wait. Luke names two. Simeon, a man in Jerusalem, "just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel." And Anna, a prophet who never left the temple, who spoke of the child "to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem." Waiting, in these pages, isn't doing nothing. It's showing up, reading, praying, keeping the customs, for years, without seeing what you're waiting for. Paul, writing later as a follower of Jesus, looks back: "when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son." Some readers hear in that word something filling slowly. And this closes a long run, from Joshua at the Jordan through judges and kings, Ruth and Samuel, David and Solomon, Elijah and Elisha, the fall and the exile, Esther, Ezra and Nehemiah, to people standing in the temple, waiting.

Bring to mind one thing you're waiting for: news, healing, a reconciliation, a change in the world or in yourself. Don't hurry it and don't give up on it; hold it the way Simeon might have, showing up one more day, and let your breath slow down around it. If you pray, bring that waiting to God; if you don't, just keep it company.
Simeon. A man in Jerusalem waiting for the consolation of Israel, one face of the long stretch between Malachi and Matthew.
Your line: the waiting years. That closes this part of the path, Joshua to the return; next, the early church. Day seven hundred forty-six, done.

howItsDone: Some Christians meet the years between the testaments through the people waiting at the start of the Gospels, like Simeon and Anna, and churches that keep Advent take up that same waiting in the weeks before Christmas.

fork.reveal: Simeon keeps coming. Luke says he came by the Spirit into the temple on the day Mary and Joseph brought the child.

chat.says: What happened between the Old and New Testaments? Were those years just silent?
options: Waiting years: Greek rule, then Rome, and synagogues where people prayed.
Nothing much happened; the people forgot God until Jesus came.
The temple stood empty, and no one gathered to pray or to read.
chat.meaning: Between Malachi and Matthew came Greek rule, then Rome, and the synagogue. People like Simeon and Anna kept showing up, waiting.

Malachi.meaning: the book on the last Old Testament page in many Bibles

synagogue.meaning: a gathering for reading and prayer

Anna.meaning: a prophet who never left the temple, and spoke of the child

Caesar Augustus.meaning: the Roman emperor whose decree opens Luke's birth story

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's 'four hundred quieter years' is not stated (no number given); the hook field reads 'the quieter centuries'. A Keeper may restore the figure if it is to be sourced.
Alexander and his successors are taken from 1 Maccabees 1:1–10; Rome from Luke 2:1. Confirm the brief summary.
'Some readers call them the silent years' is attributed, not asserted.
'Luke's Christmas story... very first line' refers to Luke 2:1 as the opening of the nativity narrative in chapter 2; confirm phrasing.
Malachi as the last book of the King James Old Testament is true of the KJV order; Orthodox ordering differs. Wording limited to the KJV.
Anna 'never left the temple' paraphrases Luke 2:37 ('departed not from the temple').
Block-end day (746): carry names the end of Block A and points to Block B, the early church.

Editor pass: hook limited to a KJV printed without the Apocrypha (with it, Malachi is not one page from Matthew); unsourced 'Jews scattered far from Jerusalem gather in synagogues' replaced by Acts 15:21 (KJV), added to sources; 'an old man' and 'waiting your whole life' (ages not in Luke 2:25) cut from teach and fork; the 'filling slowly' reading of Galatians 4:4 attributed to some readers; carry no longer calls this 'the end of Israel's story'; howItsDone 'mostly' softened.

Audit: narrator line 'Paul later puts the end of the waiting this way' stated the Christian claim (the waiting ended in Jesus) in the narrator's voice; now attributed to Paul looking back as a follower of Jesus. 'The very first line of Luke's Christmas story' (Luke's narrative opens at 1:5 with Herod) changed to 'Luke's account of the birth opens with' (2:1).
